en: The Compendium of Dharma (Dharmasaṃgraha).
Homage to the Three Jewels.
Having paid homage to the Three Jewels, which bring about the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, this Compendium of the Essence of Dharma is spoken for the destruction of delusion.
1. In that regard, first of all, there are the three jewels, namely:
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
2. The three vehicles— namely, the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and [the vehicle of the bodhisattvas].
And the Mahāyāna.
3. The five Buddhas, namely:
Vairocana, Akṣobhya, [Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi].
Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.
4. Four goddesses, namely: Rocanī, Māmakī, [Pāṇḍaravāsinī, and Tārā].
Pāṇḍurā and Tārā.
5. Five Protections: namely, Pratisarā and Sāhasrapramardanī.
Mārīcī, Mantrānusāriṇī,
and Śīlavatī.
6. The seven Tathāgatas, namely: Vipaśyin, Śikhin, [Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni].
Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni.
Kāśyapa and Śākyamuni.
7. The four world-protectors (*lokapāla*), namely: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūpākṣa, [Virūḍhaka, and Vaiśravaṇa].
Virūḍhaka and Kubera.
8. The eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*):
namely, Indra, Yama, and so forth.
Varuṇa,
Kubera,
and Īśāna.
Agni, Nairṛta, and Vāyu.
9. There are ten world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
Above the eight world-protectors is Brahmā, and below is Kṛṣṇa.
10. The fourteen world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Namely:
the entire group of ten world-protectors, Candra, and so forth.
The sun, the earth, and the asura.
11. The ten wrathful deities (*krodha*), namely:
Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, [Padmāntaka, Vighnāntaka, Acala, Takkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, Mahābala, Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, and Sumbharāja].
Padmāntaka, Vighnāntaka,
and Acalaṭarkirāja.
Nīladaṇḍa, Mahābala,
and Uṣṇīṣa.
The universal monarch and the noble king.
12. Eight bodhisattvas, namely: Maitreya, Gaganagañja, [and so forth].
Samantabhadra,
Vajrapāṇi,
and Mañjuśrī.
Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin,
Kṣitigarbha, and Khagarbha.
13. The six yoginīs, namely: Vajravārāhī, Yāminī, [Rūpiṇī, Khecarī, Cakravegā, and Ghasmarī].
Saṃcāraṇī, Saṃtrāsanī,
and Cāṇḍikā.
14. The sevenfold unsurpassed worship; namely:
prostration, ... [and so forth].
worship, confession of misdeeds, and rejoicing [in merit]
The request [to teach], the generation of the thought of awakening (bodhicittotpāda),
and the dedication (pariṇāmanā).
15. Three roots of virtue:
the generation of the mind of awakening, and the purification of one's intention.
And the relinquishing of the notions of "I" and "mine."
16. The four divine abodes (brahmavihāra):
loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), [and equanimity (upekṣā)].
And equanimity.
17. The six perfections:
the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, [the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom].
the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor,
and the perfection of meditation;
And the perfection of wisdom.
18. The ten perfections (pāramitā):
the six perfections in their entirety, along with skillful means (upāya).
Vow, power,
and knowledge.
19. The four means of integration: giving, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency between words and deeds.
And common purpose.
20. The five supernormal knowledges (pañcābhijñā):
the divine eye (divyacakṣus) and the divine ear (divyaśrotra).
Knowledge of the minds of others,
recollection of former abodes, and supernormal power.
21. The four noble truths; namely: suffering, the origin,
Cessation and the path.
22. The five aggregates:
form, feeling, perception, [volitional formations, and consciousness].
Formations and consciousness.
23. The five supramundane aggregates:
the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
24. The twelve sense bases (āyatana): the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the sense bases of visible forms, odors, sounds, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
25. The eighteen elements (dhātu).

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the elements of visible form, odor, sound, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena; as well as the elements of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—these constitute the eleven aggregates of form (rūpaskandha).
the eye, the ear,
the nose,
and the tongue.
the body, form, and sound;
Odor, taste, touch, and informative intimation.
27. Feeling is threefold: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
28. The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) consists essentially in the grasping of signs (nimitta).
29. Formations are of two kinds:
therein, formations associated with the mind and formations dissociated from the mind.
30. There are forty formations associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayuktasaṃskāra*).
They are as follows: feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth.
volition, desire,
and contact;
discernment,
mindfulness, and attention;
resolute conviction,
meditative concentration,
and faith.
heedfulness, pliancy, and equanimity.
Shame (hrī), dread of blame (apatrapā), and non-greed (alobha).
non-aversion, non-violence, and vigor;
delusion, negligence, and indolence.
lack of faith,
torpor, and restlessness.
lack of shame, lack of dread,
and anger;
Enmity, deceit, and envy.
Giving, hypocrisy, and stinginess.
Deceit, pride, and harmfulness.
Applied thought and sustained thought.
31. Among those, there are thirteen formations dissociated from mind:
acquisition (prāpti), non-acquisition (aprāpti), and homogeneity (sabhāgatā).
Non-perception,
completion,
and vitality.
Birth, aging, and duration.
impermanence,
the collection of names, and the collection of phrases.
And the collection of phonemes.
32. There are three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). They are as follows: space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and [cessation not through deliberation].
And cessation not through deliberation.
33. The six sense objects; namely: form, sound, [smell, taste, tactile object, and mental object].
odor, taste,
and touch.
And [it is] Dharma.
34. Therein, form has the nature of an object:
blue, yellow, and so forth.
red,
white, and green.
Long, short, and circular.
elevated, depressed, and even;
Wide-open,
clear, smoke.
Dust, mist, and shadow.
Namely, sunlight, light,
and darkness.
35. Sound is of twenty-eight kinds:
seven are sounds of human speech, and seven are sounds of human hands and so forth.
These same [objects], through the distinction between the agreeable and the disagreeable, constitute twenty-eight.
36. Taste is of six kinds;
namely: sweet, sour, [bitter, pungent, astringent, and salty].
Salty, pungent, and bitter.
And "astringent" (kaṣāya).
37. There are four types of odors; namely:
pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, [equal odor, and unequal odor].
Even fragrance and uneven fragrance.
38. There are eleven types of tangible objects: earth, water, fire, [wind, heaviness, lightness, smoothness, roughness, cold, hunger, and thirst].
wind,
smoothness,
and roughness.
lightness, heaviness,
and coldness.
Hunger and thirst.
39. The five great elements: earth, water, fire, [wind, and space].
Wind and space.
40. The five derivative elements:
visible form, sound, odor, [taste, and tangible object].
Taste and touch.
41. The twenty emptinesses: namely—emptiness of the internal, emptiness of the external,
internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness,
and great emptiness.
emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of the conditioned, and emptiness of the unconditioned;
absolute emptiness,
emptiness without beginning or end,
and emptiness of non-dispersal;
emptiness of intrinsic nature,
emptiness of all phenomena,
and emptiness of characteristics;
the emptiness of the uncharacterized,
the emptiness of existence,
and the emptiness of non-existence;
emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence,
and emptiness of other-nature.
42. The twelvefold dependent origination:
ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness,
name-and-form, the six sense bases, and contact;
feeling, craving, and clinging;
existence, birth,
and old age and death;
And [there are] sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
43. The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening:
the four foundations of mindfulness. // 4 //
The four right efforts. // 8 //
The four bases of psychic power. // 12 //
The five faculties. // 17 //
The five powers. // 22 //
The seven factors of enlightenment. // 29 //
And the noble eightfold path. // 37 //
44. In that regard, what are the foundations of mindfulness?
They are as follows: the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body in the body, and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings in feelings.

The application of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind with regard to the mind, and the application of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena with regard to phenomena.
45. What are the four right efforts? They are as follows: the preservation of wholesome roots that have already arisen;
and the production of those that have not yet arisen.
The abandoning of unwholesome states that have arisen,
and the non-arising again of those that have not yet arisen.

46. The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). They are as follows: the base of psychic power endowed with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) for the abandonment [of hindrances] through concentration of desire;
likewise, the base of psychic power of mind (*citta*); [the base of psychic power of energy (*vīrya*); and the base of psychic power of investigation (*mīmāṃsā*)].
The basis of psychic power consisting of energy;
and the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces for the abandonment [of hindrances] through concentration on investigation.
47. The five faculties;
namely: the faculty of faith, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, and the faculty of wisdom.
48. The five powers:
namely, the power of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
49. The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

They are as follows: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*), [the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity].
the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy,
and the factor of enlightenment of tranquility;
the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
50. The Noble Eightfold Path.
Right view, right intention, and right speech.
right action,
right effort,
and right mindfulness.
And right concentration; these are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
51. The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); namely:

the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), [the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)].
the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
52. There are four types of dhāraṇīs; namely:
the dhāraṇī of the self, the dhāraṇī of the text, and so forth.
The dhāraṇī of the Dharma and the dhāraṇī of mantras.
53. The four reliances are as follows: reliance on the meaning, not reliance on the letter;
reliance on gnosis, not reliance on consciousness.
Relying on the definitive meaning, not on the interpretable meaning;
relying on the Dharma, not on the person.
54. The six recollections:
recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, [recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the deities].
recollection of the Sangha, recollection of relinquishment,
and recollection of ethical discipline.
And the recollection of the deities.
55. The four Dharma-footings are as follows: all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
all conditioned phenomena are suffering.
All conditioned phenomena are without self;
nirvana is peace.
56. The ten unwholesome actions;
namely—killing living beings, taking what is not given, and so forth.
sexual misconduct,
false speech,
and slander;
harsh speech, frivolous chatter,
and covetousness;
Malice and wrong view.
57. There are six destinies, namely:
hell, the animal realm, and so forth.
A hungry ghost, an asura,
a human, and a deity.
58. The six elements: earth, water, fire, [wind, space, and consciousness].
Wind, space,
and consciousness.
59. The eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). They are as follows: possessing the perception of form, one sees forms as empty; having no internal perception of form, one sees external forms as empty.
He perceives the sphere of infinite space as empty;
he perceives the sphere of infinite consciousness as empty;
he perceives the sphere of nothingness as empty.
He perceives the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as empty;
he perceives the cessation of perception and feeling as empty as well.
60. The five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantaryāṇi*).
They are as follows: killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an Arhat, [and so forth].
The shedding of the Tathāgata’s blood with a malicious mind, and the schism of the Saṃgha.
61. The eight worldly dharmas.
gain, loss, pleasure,
and pain.
fame, infamy, and censure;
And there is praise as well.
62. The ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-pravacana*); namely: the discourses (*sūtra*), the mixed prose and verse (*geya*), and so forth.
prose exposition, verses, and inspired utterances;
Birth stories, extensive teachings, and marvelous events;
And there is the oral instruction.
63. The twelve ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*): being an alms-food eater (*paiṇḍapātika*),...
One who possesses only three robes, one who eats only from the alms-bowl after others have finished eating, and one who remains in a sitting posture.
One who uses whatever seat is available, one who dwells at the foot of a tree, and one who eats at a single sitting.
One who dwells in the open air, one who dwells in the forest, and one who dwells in cemeteries.
One who wears robes made of rags from dust heaps,
and one who follows the instructions of a preceptor.
64. The ten stages:
the Joyous, the Immaculate, the Radiant,
Arciṣmatī, Sudurjayā,
Abhimukhī,
Dūraṅgamā, Acalā,
and Sādhumatī.
And the Cloud of Dharma.
65. Samantaprabhā,
Nirupamā, and Jñānavatī—
these thirteen stages together constitute [the path].
66. There are five eyes: the fleshly eye, the Dharma-eye, the wisdom-eye, the divine eye, and the Buddha-eye.
The eye of wisdom,
the divine eye,
and the Buddha-eye.
67. There are six afflictions: attachment, aversion, pride, [doubt, views, and ignorance].
Ignorance, wrong view,
and doubt.
68. The five views:
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), [the view of wrong attachment, the view of holding as supreme, and the view of false views].
wrong view, adherence to views, and adherence to precepts and observances.
69. There are twenty-four secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
They are as follows: anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), and so forth.
concealment, spite, and envy;
Avarice, deceit, and guile.
Intoxication,
harmfulness, and shamelessness.
lack of moral dread,
sloth,
and lack of faith.
Laziness, heedlessness, and loss of mindfulness.
distraction, lack of clear comprehension, and remorse;
Drowsiness, applied thought, and sustained thought.
70. There are five kinds of nutriment:
the nutriment of meditative absorption, and the nutriment of physical food.
These are the nutriment of contact, the nutriment of mental volition, and the nutriment of consciousness.
71. Five fears:
fear for one's livelihood, fear of sorrow, [fear of death, fear of states of deprivation, and fear of the Dharma].
The fear of death, the fear of an evil rebirth,
and the fear of humiliation before an assembly.
72. The four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

They are as follows: the first *dhyāna* is characterized by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), and consists of the joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*).
The second [dhyāna] consists of joy and bliss arising from internal serenity (*adhyātma-pramodanāt*).
The third [dhyāna] consists of equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss;
the fourth dhyāna consists of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, and the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant.
73. There are three liberations: emptiness, the signless, and the wishless.
74. Bodhisattvas have ten masteries: mastery over life, mastery over mind, and so forth.
mastery over requisites,
mastery over the Dharma,
and mastery over supernatural powers.
Mastery over birth, mastery over resolve,
and mastery over aspiration.
Mastery over karma and mastery over gnosis.
75. The ten powers of bodhisattvas are as follows:
the power of resolute belief, the power of analytical discernment, and so forth.
the power of intention, the power of patience,
and the power of knowledge.
the power of abandonment, the power of concentration,
and the power of eloquence.
The power of merit and the power of practice.
76. The ten powers of the Tathāgata are as follows: the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, and the power of knowing the ripening of karma.
The power of knowledge of the various elements, the power of knowledge of various inclinations, and the power of knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings.
the power of knowledge regarding the practice leading to all destinations;
the power of knowledge regarding the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments;
and the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of former abodes.
The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth, and the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows.
77. The four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). They are as follows: the ground of self-confidence regarding perfect enlightenment;
The fearlessness regarding the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows,
the fearlessness regarding the entry into the path leading to nirvana, and the fearlessness regarding the definitive declaration that obstructive factors are otherwise than what they appear.
78. Five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding the Dharma, stinginess regarding gain, [stinginess regarding praise, stinginess regarding teachings, and stinginess regarding disciples].
Namely: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding wholesome qualities, and stinginess regarding praise.
79. The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikā buddhadharmāḥ*).
They are as follows: the Tathāgata has no physical lapse;
he has no vocal outcry.
There is no loss of mindfulness;
there is no unconcentrated mind;
there is no perception of diversity.
There is no equanimity that is not through discernment;
there is no loss of zeal;
there is no loss of vigor.
There is no loss of mindfulness;
there is no loss of concentration;
there is no loss of wisdom.
There is no falling away from liberation;
there is no falling away from the knowledge and vision of liberation;
all bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
The revolving of all vocal actions preceded by knowledge;
the revolving of all mental actions preceded by knowledge;
and unattached, unimpeded knowledge regarding the past time.
And in the present time, there is unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision.
80. There are four māras; namely:
the māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra), the māra of the afflictions (kleśamāra), [the māra of death (mṛtyumāra), and the māra of the son of gods (devaputramāra)].
The Māra of the sons of gods and the Māra of death.
81. There are four factors of faith;
namely: the Noble Truths and the Triple Gem.
Karma and the fruit of karma.
82. The nine successive attainments of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely:
the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
And the attainment of cessation.
83. The thirty-two marks. They are as follows: having hands and soles of the feet marked with wheels;
having hands and soles of the feet that are well-placed.
The fingers, hands, and soles of the feet are webbed;
the palms of the hands and soles of the feet are soft and youthful.
The seven protuberances; long fingers;
and broad heels.
Straightness of the limbs;
the feet being turned upward; and the body hairs pointing upward.
The legs are like those of the eṇeya deer;
the arms hang down long;
and the private parts are concealed within a sheath.
The golden complexion;
the white skin;
and the body hairs that grow singly and curl to the right.
A face adorned with the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft;
a body like that of a lion from the shoulders upward;
and well-rounded shoulders.
The space between his shoulders is level;
he has the excellence of the supreme sense of taste;
and his body is well-proportioned like a banyan tree.
The protuberance on the crown of the head;
the large tongue;
and the jaw like that of a lion.
White teeth; even teeth;
a gait with the stride of a swan.
The quality of having teeth without gaps;
the quality of having forty even teeth;
the quality of having deep blue eyes.
And having eyes like those of a cow.
84. The eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana). They are as follows: having copper-colored nails; having glossy nails.
High-tufted nails;
fingers shaped like parasols;
variegated fingers.
The fingers are tapered;
the veins are hidden;
and the veins are free of knots.
Hidden ankles; level feet;
and a gait with the stride of a lion.
The gait with the stride of an elephant;
the gait with the stride of a swan;
the gait with the stride of a bull.
Walking in a clockwise direction; walking gracefully; walking without deviation.
Roundness of the limbs;
smoothness of the limbs; and gradual tapering of the limbs.
Purity of the limbs, softness of the limbs, and clarity of the limbs.
The perfection of the secondary marks;
the broad and beautiful circularity of the limbs; and evenness of gait.
Purity of the eyes; delicacy of the limbs;
and lack of dejection in the body.
Vigor of the limbs;
depth of the abdomen;
clarity of the limbs.
The state of having well-proportioned major and minor limbs;
the state of possessing pure light free from darkness;
and the state of having a rounded belly.
A smooth abdomen; an unbent abdomen; a slender abdomen.
A navel that spirals to the right;
a state of being pleasing from all sides;
and a state of pure nobility.
The state of having limbs free from moles;
the state of having hands as soft and delicate as cotton;
and the state of having glossy lines on the palms.
The lines on the palms are deep;
the lines on the palms are long;
the mouth is not excessively long.
Lips like the bimba fruit;
a soft tongue; a slender tongue.
A red tongue;
a voice like the thundering of clouds;
and a sweet, charming, and melodious tone.
The teeth are rounded;
the teeth are sharp;
the teeth are white.
Evenness of the canine teeth;
gradual tapering of the canine teeth; and a prominent nose.
Purity of the nose,
broad eyes,
and variegated eyelashes.
The eyes have lashes like the petals of white and blue lotuses;
the eyebrows are long;
and the eyebrows are white.
The eyebrows are very smooth;
the vine-like arms are full and long; and the ears are symmetrical.
Unimpaired faculty of hearing;
a non-sunken forehead;
a broad forehead.
The head is perfectly full;
the hair is like that of a black bee;
and the hair is beautifully variegated.
The state of having curly hair;
the state of having unentangled hair;
the state of having hair that is not coarse.
Fragrant hair,
and palms and soles of the feet marked with the śrīvatsa, the svastika, and the nandyāvarta.
85. The seven jewels of a universal monarch (cakravartin) are as follows:
the wheel-jewel (cakraratna), the horse-jewel (aśvaratna), [the elephant-jewel, the jewel-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel].
the jewel of the elephant, the jewel of the gem, and the jewel of the woman;
The sword-jewel and the counselor-jewel.
86. In that regard, there are three time periods;
namely: the past time period, the future time period, and [the present time period].
And the present time as well.
87. There are four types of eons (*kalpa*): namely, intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*) and great eons (*mahākalpa*).
There are eons that are empty and eons that are substantial.
88. There are four ages (*yuga*), namely:
the Kṛta age, the Tretā age, [the Dvāpara age, and the Kali age].
The Dvāpara age and the Kali age.
89. The two worlds: namely, the world of sentient beings (sattvaloka) and the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).
90. There are four modes of birth, namely:
birth from an egg, birth from moisture, [birth from a womb, and birth by transformation].
Namely, the womb-born and the spontaneously born.
91. There are five corruptions (*kaṣāya*).

They are as follows: the corruption of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the corruption of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), [the corruption of lifespan, the corruption of sentient beings, and the corruption of the eon].
The defilement of sentient beings, the defilement of lifespan, and the defilement of the eon.
92. There are three obsessions regarding sentient beings, namely: obsession regarding the thorough knowledge of the prior limit, and obsession regarding the thorough knowledge of the posterior limit.
And for the sake of the thorough knowledge of the four crores of Māras.

93. There are ten knowledges (*jñāna*). They are as follows: the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), [the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of conventional reality, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising].
knowledge of cessation, knowledge of the path, and knowledge of phenomena.
subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge,
and knowledge of the minds of others;
The knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
94. There are five knowledges; namely:
the mirror-like knowledge (ādarśanajñāna), the knowledge of equality (samatājñāna),...
The wisdom of discernment,
the wisdom of accomplishing activities, and the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena.
95. There are two truths; namely, conventional truth and ultimate truth.

96. Within the four noble truths, there are sixteen characteristics consisting of patiences and knowledges; namely: the patience for the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering, and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering.
The receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding suffering,
the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering; the receptivity to dharma-knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering], (Dhs, Vaidya 336)
Dharma-knowledge regarding origination, receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding origination, and subsequent knowledge regarding origination.
Receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation, the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation,
and receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
Subsequent knowledge regarding cessation;
receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path,
and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path.
The receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding the path,
and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
97. Therein, regarding the truth of suffering, there are four aspects, namely: as impermanent, as suffering, [as empty, and as non-self].
As emptiness and as selflessness.

98. There are four aspects regarding the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*); namely: as cause (*hetutaḥ*), as origination (*samudayataḥ*), [as production (*prabhavataḥ*), and as condition (*pratyayataḥ*)].
From the perspective of origination and from the perspective of conditions.
99. There are four aspects regarding the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*); namely:
as cessation (*nirodhataḥ*), as peace (*śāntataḥ*), [as excellence (*praṇītataḥ*), and as liberation (*niḥsaraṇataḥ*)].
By way of excellence and by way of renunciation.
100. There are four aspects regarding the truth of the path; namely:
as the path, as the method, [as the achievement, and as the deliverance].
By way of practice and by way of leading to liberation.
101. There are four concentrations, namely:
the concentration of light, the concentration of the enclosure, ... [the concentration of the unobstructed, and the concentration of the unimpeded].
The concentration established in eleven [factors] and the uninterrupted concentration.
102. In this regard, there are eight types of persons (*pudgala*): namely, the one practicing for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*), and the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
one who has entered the path to the fruit of once-returning,
a once-returner,
and one who has entered the path to the fruit of non-returning;
the non-returner, the one practicing for the fruit of arhatship, and the arhat.
103. Likewise, there are eight types of individuals (*pudgala*), namely:
the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*) and the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārī*).
the stream-enterer, the one who goes from family to family among the gods, and the one who goes from family to family among humans;
The once-returner;

the one liberated through faith, the one attained through vision, and the one separated by a single interval; the non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon landing, the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, the leaper, the half-leaper, the one who leaps all the way, the one equal to those in the present life, the body-witness, and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha].

104. [Next, what is the turning of the wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects? It is as follows: "O monks, regarding these teachings, having previously heard that 'this is the noble truth of suffering,' through wise reflection, the eye arose."
Knowledge arose, thought arose; vision arose.
Thus, monks, this is the first turning of the wheel:
"This is suffering," O Noble Ones; this, indeed, was directly known by him. Monks!
"Thus, and so forth, as previously stated."
"This noble truth of the origin of suffering has indeed been fully understood and abandoned by you"—this and so forth is the third [turning].
Likewise, "This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering"—this is the individual [turning] for each.

"This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this indeed must be realized through higher knowledge and manifested"—this is the second [turning]. "This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this indeed must be realized through higher knowledge and manifested"—this is the second.
For example: "This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—this is the first.
"This is the noble truth that this is the practice leading to the liberation from suffering"—this, O monks, is what should be fully understood and cultivated; such is the third turning.
Thus, in this manner, there is the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects.
Thereafter, [the Buddha] turned the wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects. What are they?
"Monks, regarding this noble truth of suffering:
having previously heard it and applying wise attention to those phenomena, vision arose,
knowledge arose, and awakening arose."
It arises three times.
"Monks, this is the noble truth that 'this is suffering,' which was indeed fully understood through direct knowledge after having heard it previously and having applied systematic attention to them."
Thus ends the second [section].
"Monks, this noble truth was indeed fully understood therein," and so forth, as before. This is [the section] beginning with those words.
"This noble truth of the origin of suffering has indeed been abandoned by you through direct knowledge"—thus begins the third [turning].
Likewise, each one [thinks]: "This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering."

"This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this, indeed, must be realized through direct knowledge"—this and so forth is the second [noble truth]. "This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this, indeed, has been realized through direct knowledge"—this is the second [noble truth].
Likewise, each [of these] is as follows: "This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," and "This is the practice leading to liberation from suffering."
"Thus, O monks, regarding this Noble Truth, one must indeed realize it and teach it"—this and so forth constitutes the third turning;
thus is the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects.
Restored Text:
In this regard, what is the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects? It is: "This is the noble truth of suffering."
"Monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to phenomena unheard of before, the eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and insight arose—this is the first turning.

'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering; this, indeed, having been directly known, has been fully understood'—thus, monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to phenomena unheard of before—this is the second [turning]."
"This is the noble truth of suffering; indeed, monks, having directly known it, it has been fully understood," and so forth as before—this is the third [noble truth].
Likewise, for each [truth]: "This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering" is the first;
"This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; it must indeed be abandoned through direct knowledge" is the second;
"This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; it has indeed been abandoned through direct knowledge" and so forth is the third.
Likewise, "This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering" is the first [turning].
"This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; it must indeed be realized through direct knowledge" and so forth is the second.
"This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; it has indeed been realized through direct knowledge" is the third.

Likewise, each of these is an Noble Truth: "This is the practice leading to the path of suffering," and "This is the Noble Truth of the practice leading to liberation from suffering. In that regard, monks, it must be fully understood and cultivated; this is the second [Noble Truth].
[This is the Noble Truth of the practice leading to liberation from suffering; in that regard, it has been fully understood and cultivated; this is the third.]
105. In that regard, giving is threefold;
namely: the gift of Dharma, the gift of material goods, and—
And the gift of loving-kindness.
106. Ethical discipline is threefold; namely: the ethical discipline of the accumulations, the ethical discipline of gathering what is wholesome, and...
And the ethical discipline of acting for the welfare of sentient beings.
107. Patience is threefold; namely:
patience in the contemplation of dharmas, and patience in the endurance of suffering.
And patience for the sake of benefiting others and for the sake of the Dharma.
108. Energy is threefold; namely: the energy of armor, [the energy of application, and the energy of non-despair].
The vigor of application and the vigor of ultimate perfection.
109. Meditation is threefold; namely: meditation for the removal of faults, and meditation for dwelling in happiness.
And it is the meditation adorned with all its embellishments without exception.
110. Wisdom is threefold; namely: that consisting of hearing, that consisting of reflection, and [that consisting of cultivation].
And that which consists of cultivation.
111. Skillful means are threefold; namely: that which awakens all sentient beings, and that which accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings.
And the swift, blissful, and perfect awakening.
112. The vow is threefold; namely: that which is connected to a good rebirth, and that which is connected to the welfare of sentient beings.
And it is the purifier of the buddha-field.
113. Power is threefold; namely: that which turns back karma, that which removes afflictions, and—
And it is that which turns one away from pride, negligence, and so forth.
114. Knowledge is threefold; namely: non-conceptual, that which brings about the awakening to the equality of conceptualization, and [conceptual].
And [the knowledge] that is indirect regarding the means for the sake of the truth.
115. In that regard, there are two obscurations; namely, the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of the knowable.
116. Selflessness is twofold; namely, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
117. The equipment is twofold;
namely, the equipment of merit and the equipment of knowledge.
118. In that regard, there are six obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); namely:
laziness (*kausīdya*), pride (*māna*), and so forth.
Deceit, restlessness, and lack of application.
And the application of truth.
119. In that regard, there are eight formative forces of abandonment through practice (*pratipatti*), namely:
faith (*śraddhā*) and wisdom (*buddhi*).
exertion, pliancy,
mindfulness, and clear comprehension;
Volition and equanimity.
120. Therein are four continents, namely:
Pūrvavideha, Jambudvīpa, [Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru].
Aparagodānīya and the continent of Uttarakuru.
121. There are eight hot hells, namely:
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, and so forth.
Saṃghāta, Raurava, and Mahāraurava.
Tapana, Pratāpana,
and Avīci.
122. There are eight cold hells; namely: Arbuda, Nirarbuda, [Utpala, Padma, Mahāpadma, Hahava, Huhuva, and Pratāpana].
Aṭaṭa, Apapa, and Hāhādhara.
The utpala,
the padma, and the mahāpadma.
123. There are seven netherworlds (pātāla), namely:
Dharaṇītala, Acala, and so forth.
Mahācala,
Āpa, and Kāñcana.
Saṃjīva and Naraka; these are the two Cakravālas. 124. There are two Cakravālas.
Namely: Cakravāla and Mahācakravāla.
125. The eight mountain ranges, namely: Yugandhara, Īśādhara, [Kailāsa, Āṣāḍha, Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka, Nimindhara, and Mahāmeru].
Khadiraka, Sudarśana, and Vinataka.
Aśvakarṇa, Nimiṃdharagiri, and Sumeru.
126. There are seven oceans; namely: the salt ocean, the milk ocean, [the curd ocean, the ghee ocean, the honey ocean, the sugarcane juice ocean, and the wine ocean].
Curd,
the ocean,
and clarified butter.
Honey and liquor.
127. Therein, there are six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*); namely:
the Cāturmahārājakāyikas, [the Trāyastriṃśas, the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, and the Paranirmitavaśavartins].
the Trāyastriṃśa, Tuṣita, and Yāma [devas],
The gods who delight in emanations and those who wield power over the emanations of others.
128. There are eighteen classes of gods belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
They are as follows: the Brahmakāyikas and the Brahmapurohitas.
The Brahma-pārṣadyas,
the Mahābrahmās,
and the Parīttābhas.
the gods of Immeasurable Light, the Luminous Gods,
and those of Limited Purity;
the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, and the Puṇyaprasavas;
The Bṛhatphalas,
the Asaṃjñisattvas,
and the Avṛhas.
the Atapas, the Sudṛśas, and the Sudarśanas;
And the Akaniṣṭhas.
129. There are four classes of gods belonging to the formless realm:
those who have reached the sphere of infinite space, and those who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Those who have reached the sphere of nothingness,
and those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
130. There are three kinds of transgressions:
namely, transgression against truth, transgression against the Dharma, and [transgression against the Sangha].
And it is also non-transgression.
131. Great loving-kindness is threefold; namely: that which has truth as its object, and that which has the Dharma as its object.
Namely, with support and without support.
132. Karma is threefold; namely: that to be experienced in the present life, and that to be experienced upon rebirth.
And that which is to be experienced in a future life.
133. There are three kinds of miracles:
namely, the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), the miracle of mind-reading (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), and [the miracle of instruction].
And the miracle of instruction.
134. The eight inopportune births (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇāḥ*).
They are as follows: rebirth in hell, rebirth among animals, and so forth.
Rebirth in the realm of Yama,
rebirth in a border region,
and rebirth among long-lived deities.
Deficiency of the sense faculties,
wrong view,
and loss of enthusiasm for the generation of the thought of awakening.

135. There are three kinds of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*): namely, the conceptual construction of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), the conceptual construction of investigation (*saṃtīraṇa-vikalpa*), [and the conceptual construction of self-nature].
Conceptual construction and innate conceptual construction.
136. There are four concentrations, namely:
Śūraṅgama, Gaganagañja, and Vimalaprabha.
and the Lion’s Play.
137. The fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛta-vastu*):
namely—whether the world is eternal, and so forth.
The world is non-eternal;
it is both eternal and non-eternal;
it is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
The world is finite,
the world is infinite,
and the world is both finite and infinite.
The Tathāgata neither has an end nor is he endless after death; the Tathāgata neither exists nor does he not exist after death.
The Tathāgata exists after death and does not exist after death;
the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death;
that which is the soul is the body.
The soul is one thing and the body is another.
138. There are three roots of wholesome merit;
namely: non-hatred, non-attachment, [and non-delusion].
And non-delusion.
139. From the opposite of these, there are three unwholesome roots, namely:
greed, delusion, and [hatred].
And hatred.
140. The three trainings:
namely, the training in higher mind, the training in higher ethical discipline, and [the training in higher wisdom].
And the training in higher wisdom.
Thus ends this *Dharmasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Nāgārjuna.
